meta.title: NC Education Research Compendium
meta.scope: NC data or NC education; connected early learning and postsecondary work included.
meta.searchType: Structured initial search, not a systematic review.

studies.title: The Relationship Between Student Attendance and Achievement, Pre- and Post-COVID
studies.authors: Tom Swiderski; Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Kevin C. Bastian
studies.setting: North Carolina public elementary and middle school students; comparisons through 2023–24.
studies.findings: More days absent were associated with lower mathematics achievement. The published analysis estimates that restoring pre-pandemic attendance could account for 13–19% of the academic recovery needed in 2023–24.
studies.implications: Pair attendance recovery with instructional supports; improved attendance alone is unlikely to close learning gaps.
studies.limitations: First-differences estimates depend on modeling assumptions. The recovery scenario is a modeled projection, not an evaluated attendance intervention.
studies.gap: Which attendance supports improve learning, for which students?
studies.versionNote: Uses the 2025 article rather than the different estimates in the November 2024 working paper.

studies.title: In School, Engaged, on Track? The Effect of the Pandemic on Student Attendance, Course Grades, and Grade Retention in North Carolina
studies.authors: Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Tom Swiderski; Camille Mikkelsen; Kevin C. Bastian
studies.setting: North Carolina public school administrative records before and during the pandemic.
studies.findings: Attendance, course grades, and grade progression worsened during the pandemic. Disruptions were uneven, with larger difficulties for some middle-grade and historically marginalized student groups.
studies.implications: Monitor engagement and course progress alongside test scores when targeting recovery supports.
studies.limitations: Administrative measures and attendance recording changed during disrupted schooling. The study does not identify the effectiveness of a particular recovery program.
studies.gap: Which combinations of academic and engagement supports sustain recovery?

sources.title: Research source
sources.basis: Published article and earlier author abstract

studies.versionNote: 2025 journal article; earlier version: EdWorkingPaper 23-747.

studies.title: Student-Level Attendance Patterns Across Three Post-Pandemic Years
studies.authors: Tom Swiderski; Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Kevin C. Bastian
studies.setting: NC students in grades K–6 at baseline, followed for three years; 2016–19 versus 2021–24.
studies.findings: The share chronically absent at least once over three years rose from 17% to 38%; persistent chronic absence across all three years rose from 2.4% to 9.6%.
studies.implications: Distinguish occasional absence from repeated, intensive needs using student histories across years.
studies.limitations: The sample excludes high school students and requires observation across three years. Descriptive changes do not establish causes.
studies.gap: How should support intensity vary with the persistence of absence?
studies.versionNote: First published online February 24, 2025; assigned to a 2026 journal issue.

studies.title: The Causal Effect of Student Absences Post Pandemic: Evidence from Three School Systems
studies.authors: Yu Hung Yaow; Seth Gershenson; David Blazar; Ethan Hutt
studies.setting: North Carolina, Maryland, and one large urban district; pre- and post-pandemic comparisons.
studies.findings: Across the study settings, absences remained harmful to test performance after the pandemic, although estimated effects were modestly smaller than before.
studies.implications: Treat attendance as a continuing learning concern while checking how effects vary by setting.
studies.limitations: This is a working-paper abstract. Pooled findings are not NC-only estimates; the attainment results described for Maryland should not be transferred to NC.
studies.gap: Do NC effects differ by grade, subject, or type of absence?

studies.title: School-Based Healthcare and Absenteeism: Evidence from Telemedicine
studies.authors: Sarah Komisarow; Steven W. Hemelt
studies.setting: School telemedicine openings in three rural North Carolina districts.
studies.findings: Access to school telemedicine was associated with a 2.5 percentage-point reduction in chronic absence and about 0.8 fewer days absent; effects were concentrated among male students.
studies.implications: Consider healthcare access when investigating local attendance barriers.
studies.limitations: Three rural districts do not represent every NC context. Clinic access is not the same as an individual student receiving care.
studies.gap: What staffing, costs, and local partnerships support replication?
studies.versionNote: Published in Education Finance and Policy 19(2), 252–282 (2024); linked open working paper dates to 2023.

studies.title: Ending Early Grade Suspensions
studies.authors: Ezra Karger; Sarah Komisarow
studies.setting: Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools; a policy limiting out-of-school suspensions in grades K–2.
studies.findings: The reform reduced suspension probability by 1.4 percentage points and narrowed the Black–White suspension gap. Average test scores and disciplinary infractions did not worsen.
studies.implications: Examine alternatives to exclusion alongside classroom outcomes and disciplinary disparities.
studies.limitations: Findings concern one district and early grades. The working-paper version does not establish effects of every suspension policy or of high-school reforms.
studies.gap: Which implementation supports sustain equitable discipline over time?

studies.title: Equal Time for Equal Crime? Racial Bias in School Discipline
studies.authors: Ying Shi; Maria Zhu
studies.setting: Statewide North Carolina administrative discipline records.
studies.findings: Comparisons within incidents and across incidents involving the same students found Black students faced higher suspension probabilities or longer suspensions than comparison students, consistent with racial bias.
studies.implications: Review disciplinary decisions for comparable incidents, rather than interpreting raw group rates alone.
studies.limitations: Administrative data cannot observe every behavioral or contextual difference. The study examines disciplinary decisions, not an evaluated remedy.
studies.gap: Which changes to decision routines reduce disparities?

studies.title: The Effect of Immigration Enforcement on School Engagement: Evidence from 287(g) Programs in North Carolina
studies.authors: Laura Bellows
studies.setting: NC counties approved for 287(g) partnerships compared with counties that applied but were not approved.
studies.findings: The analysis found lower attendance after program activation, with increases in chronic absence, but no detected achievement effect.
studies.implications: Investigate community and family barriers when interpreting changes in attendance.
studies.limitations: The historical policy setting differs from current enforcement contexts. Chronic absence used a 15-day threshold, so rates are not directly comparable with today’s 10% measure.
studies.gap: Which locally appropriate family supports protect school engagement?

studies.title: What Happens When You Combine High School and College? The Impact of Early Colleges on Postsecondary Performance and Completion
studies.authors: Julie A. Edmunds; Fatih Unlu; Jane Furey; Elizabeth Glennie; Nina Arshavsky
studies.setting: 1,687 applicants to 12 North Carolina early colleges; follow-up through six years after grade 12.
studies.findings: Lottery-offered students more often earned a postsecondary credential (44.3% versus 33.0%), particularly an associate degree. The overall bachelor’s completion difference at six years was not statistically significant.
studies.implications: Consider the complete early-college model, including academic and student supports.
studies.limitations: Results apply to applicants and participating lottery schools. They do not isolate dual-credit coursework from other features of the model.
studies.gap: How do effects transfer to other schools and current student cohorts?

studies.title: CTE-Focused Dual Enrollment: Participation and Outcomes
studies.authors: Julie A. Edmunds; Fatih Unlu; Brian Phillips; Christine Mulhern; Bryan C. Hutchins
studies.setting: North Carolina students participating in CTE dual enrollment in grades 11–12.
studies.findings: About 9% participated. Participation was positively associated with college credits, high-school graduation, and college enrollment; participation disparities were smaller than in college-transfer dual enrollment.
studies.implications: Examine CTE dual enrollment as one pathway to broaden college access.
studies.limitations: Participation was not randomly assigned. The abstract supports associations and does not show that every CTE pathway produces the same benefits.
studies.gap: Which credentials and programs lead to sustained completion and employment?

programs.note: Examines participation and outcomes in the CTE dual-enrollment pathway.

studies.versionNote: Upgraded from the 2022 working paper to the accepted journal version, first cited online in 2023 and assigned to Education Finance and Policy 19(4), 612–633 (2024). DOI 10.1162/edfp_a_00414. These versions are one study family.

studies.title: The Long-Term Effect of North Carolina’s Pre-Kindergarten Program Is Larger in School Districts with Lower Rates of Growth in Academic Achievement
studies.authors: Robert C. Carr; Tyler W. Watts; Jade M. Jenkins; Yu Bai; Ellen S. Peisner-Feinberg; Clara G. Muschkin; Helen F. Ladd; Kenneth A. Dodge
studies.setting: NC birth and education records; pre-K funding exposure and achievement through grade 8.
studies.findings: Estimated benefits of NC Pre-K funding were larger in districts with slower subsequent achievement growth. Funding benefits also added to the advantages of higher average district achievement.
studies.implications: Consider early learning and later school environments together.
studies.limitations: Funding exposure is not individual program attendance. Estimates reflect historical cohorts and rely on the funding-variation design.
studies.gap: How do current pre-K and elementary supports interact?
studies.versionNote: EdWorkingPaper 21-494, revised August 2022.

programs.note: Examines NC Pre-K funding and later student outcomes.

studies.title: Effects of North Carolina’s Pre-Kindergarten Program at the End of Kindergarten: Contributions of School-Wide Quality
studies.authors: Robert C. Carr; Ellen S. Peisner-Feinberg; Rachel Kaplan; Irina L. Mokrova
studies.setting: NC Pre-K participants and comparison children followed to the end of kindergarten.
studies.findings: Average-quality elementary schools showed no reliable overall NC Pre-K effect in this analysis. Language or working-memory benefits were evident under some higher-quality school conditions; literacy and mathematics moderation was not detected.
studies.implications: Follow several developmental outcomes and the quality of children’s subsequent school environments.
studies.limitations: Observational comparisons cannot rule out all selection differences. These short-term outcomes and participation measures differ from long-term funding studies.
studies.gap: Which transitions sustain early gains for different children?

programs.note: Examines NC Pre-K participation and kindergarten outcomes.

studies.title: Math Acceleration in Elementary School: Access and Effects on Student Outcomes
studies.authors: Steven W. Hemelt; Matthew A. Lenard
studies.setting: Wake County elementary students, 2013–14 through 2017–18.
studies.findings: Girls were less likely to be nominated and qualify than similarly performing boys. Acceleration effects differed by gender, including evidence of short-term mathematics knowledge decay for girls.
studies.implications: Review nomination, qualification, and continued participation separately when expanding access.
studies.limitations: One district’s elementary single-subject acceleration policy is distinct from statewide middle-grade automatic enrollment. The findings should not be treated as universal acceleration effects.
studies.gap: What supports help students remain successful after acceleration?

studies.title: Objective Course Placement and College Readiness: Evidence from Targeted Middle School Math Acceleration
studies.authors: Shaun M. Dougherty; Joshua S. Goodman; Darryl V. Hill; Erica G. Litke; Lindsay C. Page
studies.setting: Wake County middle-school mathematics placement based on prior test scores.
studies.findings: Using an objective eligibility threshold increased later advanced mathematics participation for students near the placement cutoff, including students whom discretionary placement could overlook.
studies.implications: Combine systematic identification with support after students enter accelerated courses.
studies.limitations: Effects near one district’s threshold may differ for other students and policies. This is not an evaluation of NC’s later statewide automatic-enrollment law.
studies.gap: How do statewide implementation and student supports affect longer-term success?
studies.versionNote: Published June 2017; earlier working paper first circulated in 2015.

studies.title: The Importance of Teaching and Learning Conditions: Influences on Teacher Retention and School Performance in North Carolina
studies.authors: Barnett Berry; Kevin C. Bastian; Linda Darling-Hammond; Tara Kini
studies.setting: 2016 NC Teacher Working Conditions survey, administrative records, and 2018–19 teacher interviews and school visits.
studies.findings: Leadership, collaboration, planning time, community support, collective practice, and student conduct were positively associated with retention. Associations were often stronger in high-poverty schools.
studies.implications: Use working-conditions results to structure local conversations and improvement plans.
studies.limitations: Associations do not establish that changing a survey score causes retention. The study uses an earlier survey and predates the pandemic.
studies.gap: Do these relationships persist across current survey administrations?

sources.title: Research source
sources.locator: Exploring Working Conditions; Influences on Teacher Retention

studies.versionNote: 2021 brief summarizes a 2019 study; counted as one study family.

studies.title: 2026 Advanced Teaching Roles Evaluation Report
studies.authors: Friday Institute evaluation team; authors and contributors listed in the report
studies.design: Mixed methods; school comparison and teacher associations
studies.setting: NC Advanced Teaching Roles schools; impact analysis through 2024–25 and implementation evidence from 2025–26.
studies.findings: The evaluation reports positive schoolwide achievement estimates, strongest in mathematics, but no significant schoolwide turnover effect. Supported-teacher results and release-time patterns were less consistent.
studies.implications: Specify coaching responsibilities and monitor implementation alongside several outcomes.
studies.limitations: School comparisons are nonrandomized. The report explicitly describes its two-year teacher-level analyses as correlational, not causal.
studies.gap: Which staffing and coaching arrangements explain variation across cohorts?
studies.versionNote: October 1, 2026 annual report. The 2024 edition is also indexed as NC-044. These are related reports from the same ongoing evaluation series with overlapping data, not independent replications.

programs.note: Evaluates ATR implementation and program outcomes.

studies.title: 2024–25 State of the Teaching Profession and School Administrator Report: NCDPI Findings Summary
studies.authors: North Carolina Department of Public Instruction
studies.setting: NC’s 115 public school districts; employment between March 2024 and March 2025.
studies.findings: NCDPI reports teacher attrition of 10.11%, compared with 9.88% the previous year. The statutory vacancy measure includes some positions filled by temporarily licensed teachers or rehired retirees.
studies.implications: Separate departures, movement within the system, and unstaffed positions when planning workforce responses.
studies.limitations: This record reviews the agency’s public summary, not the full report. Definitions limit comparisons across years and with other states.
studies.gap: Where do persistent local shortages and early-career departures concentrate?

sources.title: Research source
sources.locator: March 4, 2026 release; attrition and vacancy definitions

studies.title: Beyond Prescriptive Reforms: An Examination of North Carolina’s Flexible School Restart Program
studies.authors: Lam D. Pham; Gage F. Matthews; Timothy A. Drake
studies.setting: North Carolina schools participating in the Restart model.
studies.findings: Restart showed positive mathematics effects, but no detected English language arts or non-test outcome effects. Lower teacher and principal turnover accounted for part of the mathematics estimate.
studies.implications: Examine how schools use flexibility and retain staff, rather than assuming autonomy alone produces improvement.
studies.limitations: The comparison design depends on counterfactual assumptions. Results vary across outcomes and do not isolate every component of Restart.
studies.gap: Which local uses of flexibility are most productive?
studies.versionNote: First online January 2024; June 2025 issue.

programs.note: Estimates outcomes associated with the NC Restart model.

studies.title: ESSER III Investments in North Carolina: A Preliminary Analysis of PRC 181 and PRC 182
studies.authors: Erin W. Manuel; Camille N. Mikkelsen
studies.setting: ESSER III applications from 112 traditional LEAs and 177 charter public school units submitted before November 2021.
studies.findings: Spending plans emphasized technology, personnel, academic recovery, and health and safety. Quantitative and qualitative analyses described differences in planned priorities.
studies.implications: Use plans to identify investments that need follow-up implementation and outcome evaluation.
studies.limitations: Plans are not verified expenditures or impacts. This study does not establish returns on ESSER spending or provide evidence about AI tools.
studies.gap: How did actual spending and implementation compare with plans?

programs.note: Analyzes NC ESSER III spending plans for PRC 181 and PRC 182.

studies.title: Recommendations for North Carolina’s Opportunity Scholarship Program, Pursuant to S.L. 2024-57
studies.authors: Matthew Pepper; Anna Egalite; Matthew G. Springer
studies.design: Technical and policy review; stakeholder consultation
studies.setting: NC assessment options for third- and eighth-grade Opportunity Scholarship recipients; more than 75 stakeholders consulted.
studies.findings: The report identifies tradeoffs among comparability, testing burden, and autonomy. Scores from different tests should not be treated as directly comparable across sectors.
studies.implications: Check test comparability and alignment before making cross-sector performance claims.
studies.limitations: This is an assessment-design study, not an estimate of the scholarship program’s effect on learning. Recommendations are those of the authors.
studies.gap: What assessment information can be reported validly and feasibly?
studies.versionNote: Report dated December 2025; hosted on the Collaboratory site in April 2026.

programs.note: Reviews student-assessment options for the Opportunity Scholarship Program.

studies.title: Project READS NC: Understanding LETRS Implementation
studies.authors: Paola Pilonieta and Project READS NC team
studies.setting: North Carolina teachers and administrators participating in LETRS professional learning.
studies.findings: The project summary reports knowledge and implementation challenges, including limited preparation time and perceived gaps in administrative support.
studies.implications: Pair professional learning with protected planning time and support for classroom application.
studies.limitations: The source presents preliminary survey findings. Perceptions do not establish LETRS effects on student achievement; a final analysis was not reviewed.
studies.gap: How do coaching and implementation supports change instruction and learning?
studies.dateNote: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

programs.note: Examines LETRS professional-learning implementation in NC.
LETRS supports Read to Achieve implementation; this project summary does not evaluate the entire Read to Achieve policy.

studies.title: High-Dosage Tutoring for Learning Recovery in Union County
studies.authors: Douglas Lauen and research team
studies.setting: Fourth-grade mathematics tutoring in nine Union County elementary schools; whole-grade and targeted models.
studies.findings: The public summary reports preliminary proficiency gains of 8–10 percentage points relative to comparison cohorts, with positive participant feedback.
studies.implications: Examine scheduling, tutor staffing, participation, and whole-grade versus targeted delivery.
studies.limitations: The project page does not provide a full technical analysis or uncertainty estimates. Preliminary gains should not be read as a confirmed causal effect or proven return on investment.
studies.gap: Which model is effective and affordable across NC contexts?
studies.dateNote: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

studies.title: Leading Workforce Effectiveness: Inhibiting and Supporting Factors
studies.authors: Laura Lunsford and research team
studies.setting: Eight rural NC LEAs selected from areas with relatively high or low teacher attrition.
studies.findings: Interviewees described student behavior, leadership turnover, support-service shortages, and local incentives as relevant to teacher retention.
studies.implications: Explore local organizational conditions and support capacity in retention planning.
studies.limitations: Purposeful selection and interview accounts do not establish statewide prevalence or causal effects. Findings remain preliminary in the reviewed summary.
studies.gap: Which locally feasible changes improve retention over time?
studies.dateNote: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

studies.title: Mitigating Educator Workforce Impacts Through Coaching
studies.authors: Anne Cash and research team
studies.setting: NC New Teacher Support Program participants and coaches during and after pandemic disruption.
studies.findings: The summary reports a positive relationship between program participation and retention, together with shifts in coaching time and topics.
studies.implications: Document the content and intensity of beginning-teacher coaching, not participation alone.
studies.limitations: Participation may reflect teacher or district differences. The preliminary project page does not supply a full identification strategy or isolate effective coaching components.
studies.gap: Which coaching practices support teachers in different school contexts?
studies.dateNote: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

studies.title: Implementing a Community School Framework in Rural Schools
studies.authors: Amy Swain and research team
studies.setting: University-assisted community school work at PW Moore Elementary in Elizabeth City–Pasquotank.
studies.findings: The project reports increased family engagement, event participation, and staff morale during its initial pilot.
studies.implications: Use family listening sessions and community partnerships to identify locally relevant supports.
studies.limitations: The public account is a local preliminary summary without a comparison design. Reported improvements cannot be attributed solely to the community school framework.
studies.gap: Which components transfer to other rural communities?
studies.dateNote: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

studies.title: Keeping Students Safe in the Digital World: School Monitoring Technologies
studies.authors: Florence Martin and research team
studies.setting: North Carolina K–12 school monitoring technologies and stakeholder experiences.
studies.findings: Participants perceived content filtering more favorably than protection against cyberbullying or self-harm. The summary also reports substantial unmet teacher training needs.
studies.implications: Evaluate purpose, staff preparation, privacy, and response processes when reviewing monitoring tools.
studies.limitations: Perceived effectiveness is not demonstrated prevention. The summary does not establish effects of AI-supported instruction or the accuracy of individual monitoring products.
studies.gap: What independent outcome and privacy evidence supports specific uses?
studies.dateNote: Undated project summary from the 2022–25 Collaboratory cohort. Publication date and final findings require follow-up.

studies.title: A Study of Cost Adequacy, Distribution, and Alignment of Funding for North Carolina’s K–12 Public Education System
studies.authors: Jason Willis; Kelsey Krausen; Alex B. Jacobson; Lori Taylor; Ruthie Caparas; Ryan W. Lewis; Karina Jaquet
studies.setting: North Carolina’s school funding system as analyzed in 2019.
studies.findings: The study treats funding adequacy, distribution, and alignment to student needs as connected issues. Authors recommend greater attention to higher-need students, flexibility, and predictable investment.
studies.implications: Evaluate allocation designs against student needs and local capacity as well as total dollars.
studies.limitations: The reviewed publisher summary describes an older policy analysis. It is not a current budget estimate, a current legal finding, or a causal evaluation of a proposed formula.
studies.gap: How would current funding options redistribute resources and support outcomes?

studies.title: The Growing Segmentation of the Charter School Sector in North Carolina
studies.authors: Helen F. Ladd; Charles T. Clotfelter; John B. Holbein
studies.design: Longitudinal sector analysis; student fixed effects
studies.setting: North Carolina charter and traditional public schools, 1999–2012.
studies.findings: The study documented increasing sector segmentation and racial imbalance. For the historical period studied, charter schools were not more effective on average than traditional public schools.
studies.implications: Consider enrollment composition, access, and school variation when interpreting sector averages.
studies.limitations: Although published within the search window, the data are much older. These findings should not be presented as a current estimate of charter-school performance.
studies.gap: How have access and outcomes changed under more recent policies?

programs.note: Examines the NC charter-school sector and student outcomes.

studies.title: Do Teacher Assistants Improve Student Outcomes? Evidence From School Funding Cutbacks in North Carolina
studies.authors: Steven W. Hemelt; Helen F. Ladd; Calen R. Clifton
studies.setting: NC elementary-school staffing and student records, 2001–2012.
studies.findings: The analysis finds positive teacher-assistant effects on reading and mathematics, with larger benefits for students of color and students in high-poverty schools.
studies.implications: Include teacher assistants when considering the mix of staffing investments.
studies.limitations: Historical funding and staffing variation differs from a modern randomized staffing trial. Current costs, duties, and implementation may change the value of an investment.
studies.gap: Which present-day staffing models produce benefits relative to their costs?

studies.title: Improving Teacher Retention in Pender County Schools Through a Tiered Model of Support
studies.authors: Travis E. Lewis; Kevin Taylor; Karen D. Jones
studies.design: Research–practice partnership; planned surveys and focus groups
studies.setting: Pender County Schools and East Carolina University; June 2024–June 2026 project period.
studies.findings: The September 2025 update reports partnership development, professional-learning design, and piloted instruments. Outcome analysis was forthcoming in that source.
studies.implications: Connect with the team for updated results and implementation materials.
studies.limitations: No retention impact findings were reviewed. The stated project period has ended; current completion and publication status need confirmation.
studies.gap: What do the completed analyses show about beginning-teacher retention?

studies.title: The COVID-19 Pandemic and Patterns of Postsecondary Enrollment in North Carolina
studies.authors: Daniel Klasik; Matthew G. Springer; Steven W. Hemelt; Sarah Crittenden Fuller
studies.setting: NC ninth-grade entry cohorts from 2013–2018 linked with UNC System records.
studies.findings: The reviewed project page describes questions about applications, financial aid, and college enrollment. It does not report project-specific findings.
studies.implications: Request the team’s latest brief before drawing conclusions about postsecondary changes.
studies.limitations: A project description is not evidence of impact. Broad background statements on the page were not treated as results of this project.
studies.gap: Which final findings are available, and for which student groups?
studies.dateNote: 2022 award; undated project description. Final publication status requires confirmation.

studies.title: 2026 North Carolina Teacher Working Conditions Survey: Preliminary Statewide Findings and Implications for School, District, and State Leaders
studies.authors: Shaun Kellogg
studies.publisher: NCDPI Office of Research and Promising Practices
studies.design: Descriptive survey analysis; exploratory comment topic modeling
studies.setting: Statewide licensed school-based educators; 102,640 responses and a 90.5% response rate.
studies.findings: Teachers reported strong school commitment, with 84.3% planning to stay at their school. Time, student conduct, and professional support were weaker areas; ratings differed by intended career plans.
studies.implications: Use local results and educator feedback to prioritize planning time, leadership, and support needs.
studies.limitations: Preliminary, descriptive self-reports do not establish causation or actual retention. Statewide averages mask local variation; charter participation was lower. Comment modeling is exploratory.
studies.gap: Do reported conditions and professional plans predict subsequent workforce and student outcomes?
studies.versionNote: May 2026 report; its findings are explicitly preliminary. This summary uses the EdNC-hosted copy; the author-provided board link is also listed below.
studies.authorshipNote: Individual authorship supplied by Shaun Kellogg; the report identifies the Office of Research and Promising Practices as the issuing office.

studies.title: The Selection and Evaluation of Advanced Teachers: Summative Report
studies.authors: Sarah Bausell; James Birkett; Duncan Culbreth; Brayan Diaz; Shaun Kellogg; Emily Thrasher; Robin Anderson; Lam Pham; Tamara Young; Kari Colley; Sarah Dyson; Caitlin Kearney; Liv Rau; Matthew G. Springer; David Stuit
studies.design: Mixed-methods measurement study; interviews, document review, regression, predictive modeling, and rubric development
studies.setting: North Carolina ATR programs; 103 stakeholder interviews, 47 program documents, and 106 leader questionnaires, with administrative analyses using 2023–24 outcomes.
studies.findings: Districts used varied, multistage selection processes; evaluation practices were less developed and often missed teacher-leadership responsibilities. No single selection measure consistently predicted both student achievement and supported-teacher retention. The study developed the Adult Leadership Teacher Evaluation Rubric (ALTER).
studies.implications: Align selection and evaluation with actual leadership duties, include supported-teacher feedback, and pilot ALTER before wider use. Interpret predictive measures alongside local context and professional judgment.
studies.limitations: The predictive analyses use a single-year, nonrepresentative sample with missing data and no independent external validation; associations are not causal effects. ALTER has stakeholder and content review, but its reliability and outcome-related validity still require pilot testing.
studies.gap: Does ALTER produce reliable, fair ratings across districts, and do selection measures predict outcomes in new cohorts?

sources.title: Full summative report (PDF)
sources.basis: Full report; findings, methods, limitations, and instrument development reviewed

studies.versionNote: Reviewed the public PDF posted in February 2026; the title page is undated and the filename includes 11.11.25. This selection-and-measurement study is separate from the annual ATR impact evaluation (NC-016). The studies share program data and should not be counted as independent replications.

programs.note: Examines selection and evaluation of Advanced Teachers, including ALTER development.

studies.title: Is Read to Achieve Making the Grade? An Assessment of North Carolina’s Elementary Reading Proficiency Initiative
studies.authors: Stephen R. Porter; D. T. Stallings; Sara Tova Pilzer Weiss (listed authors and contributors)
studies.design: Statewide comparison of initial implementation cohorts
studies.setting: Traditional NC public-school students first identified in 2013–14 and 2014–15; reading outcomes one and two years later.
studies.findings: The executive summary reports no statistically detectable reading-score advantage for the first two cohorts, including retained students and reading-camp participants. Implementation varied across districts.
studies.implications: Study local delivery and earlier literacy supports when interpreting the historical results.
studies.limitations: The institutional executive summary was reviewed, not the full technical report. Findings concern early implementation before the 2021 literacy reforms and do not evaluate LETRS.
studies.gap: How have outcomes changed under subsequent literacy reforms?

sources.title: Research source
sources.locator: Student Outcomes; Reading Camps; Moving Forward

programs.note: Evaluates the first cohorts under the original Read to Achieve policy.

studies.versionNote: 2018 evaluation of early program cohorts. The older PDF host could not be retrieved securely; the Friday Institute executive summary supplies the reviewed evidence.

studies.title: Examining the Small-Group Reading Instruction of K–5 Teachers Who Completed Science of Reading-Aligned Professional Development
studies.authors: Alicia A. Stewart; Paola Pilonieta; Erin K. Washburn; Brittany S. Hart
studies.setting: 47 volunteer teachers from 33 NC districts; 83 K–5 lesson videos after LETRS completion.
studies.findings: Lessons included explicit instruction and modeling, alongside continued practices inconsistent with reading research. Observed differences by grade and reading level were not statistically significant.
studies.implications: Pair professional learning with observation, feedback, and support for classroom application.
studies.limitations: Volunteers and limited lesson samples restrict generalization. There was no pretraining comparison, so the study cannot estimate LETRS effects; the observation tool also needs validation.
studies.gap: Which implementation supports improve instruction and student reading?

programs.note: Observes instruction among NC teachers who completed LETRS.
Examines a training component of literacy reform, not the whole Read to Achieve policy.

studies.title: An Analysis of the Effects of North Carolina’s Opportunity Scholarship Program on Student Achievement
studies.authors: Anna J. Egalite; D. T. Stallings; Stephen R. Porter
studies.setting: Volunteer public- and private-school students tested in 2017; preferred new-recipient analysis used 245 students.
studies.findings: New scholarship recipients had positive mathematics and language estimates, but no detectable reading effect. Positive estimates were concentrated in private schools using the same test family.
studies.implications: Check sample coverage and test comparability before applying estimates to statewide policy.
studies.limitations: Nonrandom, nonrepresentative volunteers attended religious private schools. Selection and test familiarity may explain differences; results do not estimate outcomes under today’s expanded eligibility.
studies.gap: What do representative, comparable assessments show for current participants?

programs.note: Estimates achievement differences for early scholarship recipients.

studies.versionNote: Published March 2020; earlier 2018 evaluation reports are related outputs, not additional independent studies.

studies.title: Long-Term Effects of Early Childhood Programs Through Eighth Grade: Do the Effects Fade Out or Grow?
studies.authors: Yu Bai; Helen F. Ladd; Clara G. Muschkin; Kenneth A. Dodge
studies.setting: Nearly 900,000 NC middle-school students; county-level Smart Start and More at Four funding exposure.
studies.findings: Higher funding exposure was associated with better reading and mathematics outcomes and less special-education placement and grade repetition through middle school. More at Four associations were larger for economically disadvantaged students.
studies.implications: Consider sustained outcomes and the surrounding early-childhood system when reviewing pre-K investment.
studies.limitations: Observational funding exposure is not individual enrollment or random assignment. Other county changes remain possible explanations; More at Four operated alongside Smart Start.
studies.gap: Do benefits persist in recent cohorts and later schooling?

studies.versionNote: Published in 2020; the manuscript was deposited in PMC in 2023. Related NC Pre-K funding analyses can share cohorts and are not independent replications.

studies.title: Social Returns to Private Choice? Effects of Charter Schools on Behavioral Outcomes, Arrests, and Civic Participation
studies.authors: Andrew McEachin; Douglas Lee Lauen; Sarah Crittenden Fuller; Rachel M. Perera
studies.setting: NC ninth-grade cohorts entering high school in 2004–05 through 2011–12; linked adult records.
studies.findings: Students entering charter schools from traditional public schools had favorable absence, suspension, conviction, and voting estimates. Results were less consistent for students already in the charter sector.
studies.implications: Distinguish entry decisions and outcomes beyond test scores when examining school choice.
studies.limitations: Nonrandom sector choices may leave unmeasured differences. Historical cohorts and linked NC records limit generalization to current schools and people outside the records.
studies.gap: Do patterns persist for recent entrants and different school models?

programs.note: Examines NC secondary charter-school attendance and later outcomes.

studies.versionNote: March 2020 accepted manuscript, forthcoming in Economics of Education Review; working-paper and journal versions are one study family.

studies.title: The Role of Course Delivery Modality in Dual Enrollment
studies.authors: Julie A. Edmunds; Brian Phillips; Christine Mulhern; Nina Arshavsky; Bryan C. Hutchins
studies.design: Propensity-weighted outcomes analysis with qualitative evidence
studies.setting: Statewide NC academic and CTE dual enrollment delivered online, on college campuses, or at high-school/other locations.
studies.findings: All three delivery groups had favorable postsecondary enrollment and credential estimates versus nonparticipants. Course pass rates differed; online CTE had the lowest pass rates.
studies.implications: Consider course completion supports alongside access when selecting delivery formats.
studies.limitations: Only the author abstract was reviewed. Comparisons are with nonparticipants, not randomized head-to-head modality assignments; results do not establish the best format for each student.
studies.gap: Which delivery supports improve success for students facing access barriers?

programs.note: Examines delivery formats within NC dual enrollment.

studies.versionNote: EdWorkingPaper 26-1523, July 2026. Shares the CCP evaluation partnership with other indexed pathway studies; it is a distinct delivery analysis, not an independent program replication.

studies.title: Career and College Promise College Transfer Pathway: Postsecondary Attainment and Employment Outcomes
studies.authors: CCP Evaluation Partnership (UNC Greensboro, RAND, and NC agency partners)
studies.setting: Postsecondary brief: NC high-school cohorts from 2012–19. Earnings brief: about 232,000 students entering grade 11 in 2012–14.
studies.findings: The briefs report favorable college-enrollment and credential outcomes. A later employment brief reports higher recorded annual and cumulative wages for College Transfer participants.
studies.implications: Follow both education and employment outcomes when examining pathway benefits.
studies.limitations: Briefs give limited technical detail. Nonrandom participation remains a concern. NC unemployment-insurance records omit out-of-state, federal, and self-employment; missing wage records are coded zero.
studies.gap: How sensitive are results to unobserved selection and missing employment sectors?

studies.title: Why Do Students Participate (or Not) in Dual Enrollment?
studies.authors: Bryan C. Hutchins; Nina Arshavsky; Julie Edmunds; Laura Rosof
studies.design: Qualitative interviews and student focus groups
studies.setting: 2020 visits to four NC high schools; 27 staff and 63 students, including eligible nonparticipants.
studies.findings: Participants valued savings, challenge, and career exploration. Awareness, advising, remaining costs, transportation, scheduling, and course availability could limit participation.
studies.implications: Address practical access barriers alongside tuition and eligibility.
studies.limitations: A small purposive qualitative sample explains experiences, not prevalence or causal effects. Interviews reflect 2020 conditions.
studies.gap: Which changes remove barriers for eligible nonparticipants?

programs.note: Examines participation in College Transfer and CTE dual enrollment.

studies.versionNote: 2023 brief within the CCP evaluation partnership; qualitative findings are distinct from, but connected to, its outcome studies.

studies.title: CARES Intensive Intervention Coaching Pilot: Findings in NCDPI’s 2025 Low-Performing Schools Report
studies.authors: North Carolina Department of Public Instruction; summarizing EPIC evaluation findings
studies.design: Agency summary of emerging evaluation findings
studies.setting: ESSER-funded NC intensive coaching pilot launched in 2021 and concluded in September 2024.
studies.findings: Educators reported stronger instructional and leadership routines. School exits from low-performing status were unstable across years and driven largely by growth-status changes.
studies.implications: Plan for sustained coaching and examine outcome trajectories beyond a single accountability designation.
studies.limitations: The report summarizes emerging findings and does not present a full comparison design. Descriptive status changes do not establish coaching effects or effects of ESSER funding overall.
studies.gap: Are gains sustained after intensive coaching ends?

studies.title: Advanced Teaching Roles Class Size Report
studies.authors: North Carolina Department of Public Instruction
studies.setting: District ATR rosters aligned with NC student-information-system class-size records.
studies.findings: The report proposes team-level student-to-teacher ratios that account for leadership release time. A small, one-year Classroom Excellence analysis found no clear class-size relationship with teacher growth scores.
studies.implications: Capture team membership and release time when describing staffing arrangements.
studies.limitations: A very small observational sample and one year of data cannot establish that larger classes are harmless. Recommendations and technology plans are not evidence of implementation or effects.
studies.gap: How do team ratios and coaching time relate to outcomes over multiple years?

studies.title: 2024 Advanced Teaching Roles Annual Evaluation Report
studies.authors: Sarah Bausell; Shaun Kellogg; Emily Thrasher; Lam Pham; Tamara Young
studies.design: Mixed methods; matched staggered difference-in-differences and district case studies
studies.setting: NC ATR programs: 2023–24 implementation across 17 PSUs, Wilson and Pitt case studies, and impact analysis through 2022–23.
studies.findings: School-level estimates were positive and significant in mathematics, while overall ELA, science, and teacher-turnover differences were not significant. Gains were stronger in earlier implementation cohorts. District case studies identified role clarity and release-time challenges.
studies.implications: Clarify responsibilities and protect time for coaching while tracking outcomes over several implementation years.
studies.limitations: School comparisons are nonrandomized and average across varied models. Teacher-level results use one year and a small PSU sample and are explicitly non-causal. Voluntary surveys and two district case studies limit generalization.
studies.gap: Which coaching arrangements explain sustained gains and variation across districts?

RA-002.headline: Early-learning findings depend on exposure and later context.
RA-002.summary: NC Pre-K studies use both participant and county-funding designs. The added middle-school follow-up reports sustained favorable funding associations; kindergarten findings remain more conditional. Shared cohorts and funding data limit independence across papers.
RA-002.practice: Track several outcomes and distinguish funding exposure from enrollment.
RA-002.gap: Test recent cohorts and later outcomes.

RA-003.headline: Systematic placement can open later mathematics pathways.
RA-003.summary: Wake County’s targeted middle-school acceleration study offers evidence about students near a test-score cutoff. It does not answer every question about grade 8 placement statewide.
RA-003.practice: Review identification and continued course success together.
RA-003.gap: What happens under current statewide rules?

RA-004.headline: Eligibility alone does not ensure access.
RA-004.summary: CCP research adds delivery and participation evidence: advising, remaining costs, schedules, and transportation shape opportunities. These qualitative findings complement, rather than establish, effects of changing access rules.
RA-004.practice: Review practical participation barriers as well as eligibility.

RA-005.headline: Pathway benefits vary by model and outcome.
RA-005.summary: Early-college lottery evidence supports credential attainment. CCP analyses add favorable education and recorded-earnings associations, with selection and employment-data limits. They do not establish that one pathway or delivery format is best.
RA-005.practice: Match decisions to the pathway, population, and outcome studied.
RA-005.gap: Extend follow-up and improve coverage of employment outside NC wage records.

RA-006.headline: School-sector results differ across outcomes and entry decisions.
RA-006.summary: Charter research adds behavioral and civic outcomes for historical ninth-grade entrants. The early Opportunity Scholarship study reports positive estimates with strong volunteer-sample and test-comparability limits. Neither establishes current sector-wide superiority.
RA-006.practice: Examine access, entry decisions, and variation within sectors.
RA-006.gap: Update representative outcomes for current eligibility and school contexts.

RA-008.headline: Statewide indicators and rural accounts answer different workforce questions.
RA-008.summary: The agency summary provides recent attrition measures; rural interviews add local perspectives on why retention can be difficult. Together they identify issues for follow-up rather than proving a retention strategy works.
RA-008.practice: Pair local staffing data with structured staff conversations.
RA-008.gap: Identify persistent shortages and evaluate responses.

RA-009.headline: Working conditions connect to retention and teachers’ plans.
RA-009.summary: Earlier NC research links workplace conditions to observed retention. The 2026 TWC report adds descriptive evidence about intended career plans; rural interviews provide context. These different measures should be interpreted separately.
RA-009.practice: Use survey results with local staffing data and educator feedback to select improvement priorities.
RA-009.gap: Test whether current conditions and reported plans predict subsequent retention.

RA-010.headline: Staffing measures need to reflect team responsibilities.
RA-010.summary: Teacher-assistant and ATR studies address different staffing arrangements. The ATR class-size report proposes team ratios that include release time, but its small one-year analysis cannot establish class-size effects.
RA-010.practice: Record team roles, caseloads, and release time alongside headcounts.
RA-010.gap: Validate staffing measures and examine outcomes across years.

RA-011.headline: Professional learning needs support for classroom application.
RA-011.summary: ATR and coaching sources examine different forms of support. New LETRS observations describe instructional strengths and remaining problems after training, without estimating training effects. ALTER still needs pilot validation; CARES findings remain preliminary.
RA-011.practice: Use feedback and observation alongside training and role-based evaluation.
RA-011.gap: Which supports change practice and sustain student and workforce benefits?

RA-014.headline: Program results depend on the version and outcome evaluated.
RA-014.summary: The collection now includes early Read to Achieve and Opportunity Scholarship evaluations, early-childhood funding research, and ATR and Restart studies. Their populations, policy periods, and designs differ; agency summaries are not independent impact replications.
RA-014.practice: Match the evidence to the policy version and intended outcome.
RA-014.gap: Add comparable implementation and cost evidence.

RA-015.headline: Implementation studies identify barriers that outcome averages can miss.
RA-015.summary: LETRS observations, CCP interviews, and preliminary coaching reports describe how support and access work in practice. Such evidence helps define improvement questions but does not establish that a proposed change causes better outcomes. ATR annual case studies add district-specific evidence about roles and coaching time.
RA-015.practice: Track participation, instructional use, staffing, and ongoing support.
RA-015.gap: Link implementation measures to credible outcome comparisons.

RA-016.headline: Average results can conceal differences across students and settings.
RA-016.summary: The indexed early-learning and mathematics studies illustrate variation by context, outcome, or student group. Subgroup findings require careful attention to the underlying design.
RA-016.practice: Check whose experience a study actually represents.
RA-016.gap: Which supports explain differences rather than merely describe them?

RA-017.headline: Effectiveness and affordability need to be examined together.
RA-017.summary: Teacher-assistant research offers historical staffing evidence. The tutoring project is investigating delivery models, but a complete cost comparison was not reviewed here.
RA-017.practice: Request current cost and staffing assumptions before scaling.
RA-017.gap: Comparable contemporary cost-per-outcome estimates remain a search priority.

RA-029.headline: Local engagement practices warrant further evaluation.
RA-029.summary: The community-school pilot describes family engagement during local implementation. It offers ideas to examine rather than a comparative effectiveness ranking.
RA-029.practice: Start with family listening and locally identified barriers.
RA-029.gap: Which approaches work in different communities?

RA-030.headline: Different safety practices require different outcome measures.
RA-030.summary: Discipline reform and digital monitoring address different risks. The indexed evidence distinguishes observed disciplinary outcomes from perceived technology effectiveness.
RA-030.practice: Define the intended safety outcome before selecting a practice.
RA-030.gap: Which approaches improve safety while preserving inclusion and privacy?

RA-031.headline: Healthcare access may be one route to stronger attendance.
RA-031.summary: A rural telemedicine study offers evidence about school-based healthcare access. It does not establish the effectiveness of all behavioral-health initiatives.
RA-031.practice: Assess local service barriers and partnerships.
RA-031.gap: Examine costs and effects across additional NC settings.

RA-036.headline: Tutoring evidence is promising but preliminary here.
RA-036.summary: The Union County summary reports favorable early outcomes. Its public project page does not provide the full analysis needed for a confident transfer or scaling decision.
RA-036.practice: Ask about tutor preparation, dosage, and delivery conditions.
RA-036.gap: Review final methods, uncertainty, and cost results.

RA-038.headline: Pathway models, course delivery, and access barriers are distinct.
RA-038.summary: Early-college and CCP evidence spans credentials, employment, modality, and participation experiences. Related outputs from the same evaluation partnership should not be counted as independent replications.
RA-038.practice: Review the supports surrounding coursework alongside access and completion.
RA-038.gap: Follow recent students across education and employment settings.

RA-041.headline: Attendance matters, and its causes and remedies differ.
RA-041.summary: NC studies document persistent absence, learning associations, and particular healthcare or policy pathways. A historical charter-entry study adds favorable attendance estimates for that choice context; it does not establish a universal attendance intervention.
RA-041.practice: Combine longitudinal monitoring with investigation of local barriers.
RA-041.gap: Evaluate which supports work for persistent absence in different settings.

RA-042.headline: Discipline decisions can change without worsening average outcomes.
RA-042.summary: Early-grade reform and disparity studies address exclusion and fairness. A separate historical charter-entry study adds behavioral outcomes, but does not identify which discipline practices explain its estimates.
RA-042.practice: Monitor both outcomes and fairness when reviewing discipline.
RA-042.gap: Replication, older grades, and implementation supports need attention.

RA-043.headline: Student-service access can support engagement.
RA-043.summary: The indexed rural telemedicine study connects healthcare access to attendance. It leaves broader questions about counselors, psychologists, nurses, and social workers unresolved.
RA-043.practice: Map service access against locally observed needs.
RA-043.gap: Compare staffing, access, and outcomes across service models.

RA-044.headline: Survey findings and local accounts offer different views of climate.
RA-044.summary: Working-conditions research, the 2026 TWC report, and a community-school pilot provide complementary perspectives. Staff perceptions and intentions should be distinguished from measured workforce and student outcomes.
RA-044.practice: Examine local variation and use multiple perspectives when interpreting climate.
RA-044.gap: Link student and staff measures to subsequent outcomes.

RA-045.headline: Family engagement evidence in this collection is local and preliminary.
RA-045.summary: The rural community-school pilot offers an implementation example. Comparative evidence across family-engagement approaches has not yet been assembled here.
RA-045.practice: Adapt ideas with families and community partners.
RA-045.gap: Broaden evidence across rural contexts and caregiver groups.

RA-046.headline: Recovery needs extend beyond test performance.
RA-046.summary: Attendance and engagement studies document persistent barriers; tutoring and preliminary CARES findings add specific intervention examples. Agency-reported coaching findings do not establish the overall effects of pandemic relief.
RA-046.gap: Evidence on disaster recovery and long-term resilience needs expansion.

RA-048.headline: Comparable measurement is central to credible comparisons.
RA-048.summary: The Opportunity Scholarship assessment review is complemented by a historical achievement study whose estimates depend partly on the test family used by participating schools. That study does not identify one universally best assessment.
RA-048.practice: Specify the interpretation and check assessment alignment.
RA-048.gap: How can representative comparisons use feasible, comparable measures?

RA-052.headline: Useful reporting requires clear comparisons and calculation rules.
RA-052.summary: The assessment review addresses cross-sector comparisons. The 2026 TWC report provides a workforce-reporting example, documenting response denominators and aggregation. These sources address distinct reporting needs.
RA-052.practice: Make calculation rules, missing responses, and subgroup coverage visible alongside results.
RA-052.gap: Evaluate which reporting approaches support valid local decisions.

RA-055.headline: Allocation evidence should connect resources, needs, and outcomes.
RA-055.summary: The initial sources cover historical finance analysis, teacher-assistant staffing, and planned ESSER priorities. These measures do not provide a current causal comparison of funding formulas.
RA-055.practice: Distinguish planned spending, actual staffing, and outcomes.
RA-055.gap: Add recent distribution analyses and evaluated policy changes.

RA-056.headline: Access policies can shape who enters an opportunity.
RA-056.summary: Mathematics, school-choice, and CCP work address different entry processes. New CCP interviews describe practical access barriers; the historical voucher analysis has a selective sample and does not establish outcomes under current eligibility rules.
RA-056.practice: Review eligibility rules alongside enrollment composition.
RA-056.gap: Update policy effects using recent cohorts.

RA-057.headline: Operational flexibility requires clear roles and measurement.
RA-057.summary: ATR and Restart studies address specific models. The separate ATR staffing report explains team ratios and data needs; it does not establish that larger classes are harmless or that a ratio rule improves outcomes.
RA-057.practice: Document staffing decisions, release time, and actual implementation.
RA-057.gap: Test current role and staffing approaches with stronger longitudinal evidence.

RA-059.headline: Policy tradeoffs include access, resources, and community effects.
RA-059.summary: The indexed finance review and immigration-enforcement study examine distinct distributional issues. They inform selected dimensions rather than a comprehensive ranking of policies.
RA-059.practice: Specify which students and communities a decision may affect.
RA-059.gap: Add current NC evidence about alternative policies.

RA-060.headline: Monitoring requires consistent definitions and follow-through.
RA-060.summary: Agency workforce reporting and ESSER-plan analysis illustrate useful descriptive monitoring. Descriptive trends and plans alone cannot determine whether a policy caused improvement.
RA-060.practice: Link plans, implementation, and subsequent outcomes.
RA-060.gap: Which monitoring systems support credible continuation decisions?

RA-061.headline: Funding design needs a current distributional analysis.
RA-061.summary: The indexed 2019 finance study offers a framework for considering adequacy and alignment. It does not simulate a current weighted-student formula.
RA-061.practice: Check the assumptions behind each allocation scenario.
RA-061.gap: Model present-day student needs and local fiscal capacity.

RA-064.headline: Targeted placement evidence is relevant but not a statewide evaluation.
RA-064.summary: Wake County’s earlier threshold-based approach offers a related NC example. It should not be described as an evaluation of the later statewide policy.
RA-064.practice: Review eligibility, opt-outs, and course persistence.
RA-064.gap: Evaluate the present statewide automatic-enrollment policy.

RA-066.headline: Restart provides one NC example of operational flexibility.
RA-066.summary: Its outcome pattern varies across subjects and measures. The model should be studied as implemented, rather than equated with every innovative-school approach.
RA-066.practice: Document how flexibility changes instruction and staffing.
RA-066.gap: Which implementation choices explain differences across schools?

RA-019.headline: A partnership is building a model for beginning-teacher support.
RA-019.summary: The Pender County project update documents design and preparation. No retention impact findings were reviewed.
RA-019.practice: Contact the team for completed analyses.
RA-019.gap: Obtain final results before classifying effectiveness.

RA-028.headline: Delivery formats offer opportunities with different support needs.
RA-028.summary: The NC dual-enrollment modality abstract reports favorable postsecondary outcomes across formats versus nonparticipation, while pass rates differ. It is not a randomized comparison of online and in-person provision.
RA-028.practice: Pair delivery choices with course-success supports.
RA-028.gap: Which supports improve success within each format?

RA-058.headline: Staffing rules require usable linked information.
RA-058.summary: The ATR class-size report identifies the need to link teacher leaders, supported teachers, students, and release time for team-level reporting. It offers a feasibility approach, not a tested estimate of reduced burden.
RA-058.practice: Check what can be recorded and maintained before changing reporting rules.
RA-058.gap: How much administrative effort does the new approach require?
